Main article: [2022 FIFA World Cup final](/wiki/2022_FIFA_World_Cup_final "2022 FIFA World Cup final")

The final was played on 18 December between Argentina and France. Both teams had won the event twice previously.[[227]](#cite_note-final1-248) Early goals from Lionel Messi and [Ángel Di María](/wiki/%C3%81ngel_Di_Mar%C3%ADa "Ángel Di María") gave Argentina a 2–0 lead against the French.[[227]](#cite_note-final1-248)[[228]](#cite_note-final2-249) Despite substitutions in the first half, France did not record a shot until after the 70th minute but were energised by additional substitutions in the 71st. A few minutes later, France were awarded a penalty as [Randal Kolo Muani](/wiki/Randal_Kolo_Muani "Randal Kolo Muani") was brought down in the penalty area by [Nicolás Otamendi](/wiki/Nicol%C3%A1s_Otamendi "Nicolás Otamendi"). Mbappé scored the penalty and added a second goal less than two minutes later to equalise the scores.[[228]](#cite_note-final2-249) With the score tied at two goals apiece, the match went to extra time. Messi scored his second goal in the 108th minute, once again giving Argentina the lead. However, Mbappé was awarded a second penalty in the 115th minute after his shot hit the arm of [Gonzalo Montiel](/wiki/Gonzalo_Montiel "Gonzalo Montiel"). Mbappé scored his third goal, becoming the second player ever to complete a [hat-trick](/wiki/Hat-trick "Hat-trick") in the final of a World Cup after [Geoff Hurst](/wiki/Geoff_Hurst "Geoff Hurst") for England in [1966](/wiki/1966_FIFA_World_Cup "1966 FIFA World Cup").[[228]](#cite_note-final2-249) With the score tied at 3–3, the match was determined via a penalty shootout. Argentina won the final after scoring all of their penalties, winning 4–2.[[228]](#cite_note-final2-249) This marked their third World Cup win and their first since [1986](/wiki/1986_FIFA_World_Cup "1986 FIFA World Cup"), and also the second team (after [Spain](/wiki/Spain_national_football_team "Spain national football team") in [2010](/wiki/2010_FIFA_World_Cup "2010 FIFA World Cup")) to win the tournament after having lost their opening game.[[228]](#cite_note-final2-249)

After announcing [his candidacy](/wiki/Jimmy_Carter_1976_presidential_campaign "Jimmy Carter 1976 presidential campaign") in [1976](/wiki/1976_United_States_presidential_election "1976 United States presidential election"), Carter secured the [Democratic nomination](/wiki/1976_Democratic_National_Convention "1976 Democratic National Convention") as a [dark horse](/wiki/Dark_horse "Dark horse") little known outside his home state before narrowly defeating [Republican](/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)") incumbent [Gerald Ford](/wiki/Gerald_Ford "Gerald Ford") in the general election.

As president, Carter [pardoned all Vietnam draft evaders](/wiki/Proclamation_4483 "Proclamation 4483") and negotiated major foreign policy agreements, including the [Camp David Accords](/wiki/Camp_David_Accords "Camp David Accords"), the [Panama Canal Treaties](/wiki/Panama_Canal_Treaties "Panama Canal Treaties"), and the second round of [Strategic Arms Limitation Talks](/wiki/Strategic_Arms_Limitation_Talks "Strategic Arms Limitation Talks"), and he [established diplomatic relations with China](/wiki/Joint_Communiqu%C3%A9_on_the_Establishment_of_Diplomatic_Relations "Joint Communiqué on the Establishment of Diplomatic Relations"). He created a national energy policy that included conservation, price control, and new technology.

As of 2000, smoking was practiced by around 1.22 billion people. At current rates of 'smoker replacement' and market growth, this may reach around 1.9 billion in 2025.[[64]](#cite_note-HNPGuindonBoisclair13-16-64)

Smoking may be up to five times more prevalent among men than women in some communities,[[64]](#cite_note-HNPGuindonBoisclair13-16-64) although the gender gap usually declines with younger age.[[15]](#cite_note-WomenTobaccoChallenges5-6-15)[[16]](#cite_note-2001SurgeonGeneralWomen47-16) In some developed countries smoking rates for men have peaked and begun to decline, while for women they continue to climb.[[65]](#cite_note-65)

As of 2002, about twenty percent of young teenagers (13–15) smoked worldwide. 80,000 to 100,000 children begin smoking every day, roughly half of whom live in Asia. Half of those who start smoking in [adolescent](/wiki/Adolescent "Adolescent") years are projected to go on to smoke for 15 to 20 years.[[13]](#cite_note-WHO2002FactSheet-13) As of 2019 in the United States, roughly 800,000 high school students smoke.[[66]](#cite_note-66)

The [World Health Organization](/wiki/World_Health_Organization "World Health Organization") (WHO) states that "Much of the disease burden and premature mortality attributable to tobacco use disproportionately affect the poor". Of the 1.22 billion smokers, 1 billion of them live in developing or transitional economies. Smoking rates have leveled off or declined in the [developed world](/wiki/Developed_world "Developed world").[[67]](#cite_note-67) In the [developing world](/wiki/Developing_world "Developing world"), however, tobacco consumption is rising by 3.4% per year as of 2002.[[13]](#cite_note-WHO2002FactSheet-13)

The first evidence of helium was observed on August 18, 1868, as a bright yellow line with a [wavelength](/wiki/Wavelength "Wavelength") of 587.49 nanometers in the [spectrum](/wiki/Emission_spectrum "Emission spectrum") of the [chromosphere](/wiki/Chromosphere "Chromosphere") of the [Sun](/wiki/Sun "Sun"). The line was detected by French astronomer [Jules Janssen](/wiki/Pierre_Janssen "Pierre Janssen") during [a total solar eclipse](/wiki/Solar_eclipse_of_August_18,_1868 "Solar eclipse of August 18, 1868") in [Guntur](/wiki/Guntur "Guntur"), India.[[26]](#cite_note-frnch-27)[[27]](#cite_note-nbb-28) This line was initially assumed to be [sodium](/wiki/Sodium "Sodium"). On October 20 of the same year, English astronomer [Norman Lockyer](/wiki/Norman_Lockyer "Norman Lockyer") observed a yellow line in the solar spectrum, which he named the D3 because it was near the known D1 and D2 [Fraunhofer lines](/wiki/Fraunhofer_line "Fraunhofer line") of sodium.[[28]](#cite_note-Lockyer_1868-29)[[29]](#cite_note-enc-30) He concluded that it was caused by an element in the Sun unknown on Earth. Lockyer named the element helium, from the Greek word for the Sun, [ἥλιος](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/en:%E1%BC%A5%CE%BB%CE%B9%CE%BF%CF%82 "wikt:en:ἥλιος") (*[helios](/wiki/Helios "Helios")*).[[30]](#cite_note-31)[[31]](#cite_note-32) It is sometimes said that English chemist [Edward Frankland](/wiki/Edward_Frankland "Edward Frankland") was also involved in the naming, but this is unlikely as he doubted the existence of this new element. The ending "-ium" is unusual, as it normally applies only to metallic elements; probably Lockyer, being an astronomer, was unaware of the chemical conventions.[[32]](#cite_note-jensen-33)
